{{Short description|Subject area matching a person's skills or expertise}}
[[File:Circle of competence.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|[[Euler diagram]] showing the actual circle of competence compared to the perceived circle, for an individual who overestimates their level of competence]]

A '''circle of competence''' is the subject area which matches a person's [[skill]]s or [[expert|expertise]].<ref name="BI">
{{cite web 
 |title=The 'Circle Of Competence' Theory Will Help You Make Vastly Smarter Decisions
 |url=http://www.businessinsider.com/the-circle-of-competence-theory-2013-12
 |accessdate=13 January 2018
 |website=[[Business Insider]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Robinson
 |first1=Bernard E.
 |title=The Skills of an Effective Leader: Becoming a Leader Others Want to Follow 
 |date=May 12, 2016|publisher=Xlibris Corporation 
 |isbn=9781514483541 
 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zwU8DAAAQBAJ 
 |accessdate=13 January 2018
}}</ref> The concept was developed by [[Warren Buffett]] and [[Charlie Munger]] as what they call a [[mental model]], a codified form of business acumen, concerning the investment strategy of limiting one's [[investment|financial investments]] in areas where an individual may have limited understanding or experience, while concentrating in areas where one has the greatest familiarity.<ref name="BI"/><ref>
{{cite web
 |title=Mental Models: The Best Way to Make Intelligent Decisions (113 Models Explained) 
 |url=https://www.farnamstreetblog.com/mental-models/ 
 |website=Farnam Street 
 |accessdate=13 January 2018
}}</ref> The strategy emphasizes the importance of aligning one's subjective assessment with actual competence.<ref name=BI/> Buffett summarized the concept in the motto, "Know your circle of competence, and stick within it. The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital."<ref>{{cite book|last1=Dobelli|first1=Rolf|title=The Art of the Good Life: 52 Surprising Shortcuts to Happiness, Wealth, and Success|date=Nov 7, 2017|publisher=Hachette Books|isbn=9780316445092|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EJUpDwAAQBAJ|accessdate=13 January 2018}}</ref>

In his 1996 letter to [[Berkshire Hathaway]], Buffett further expanded:

<blockquote>
What an investor needs is the ability to correctly evaluate selected businesses. Note that word 'selected': You don't have to be an expert on every company, or even many. You only have to be able to evaluate companies within your circle of competence.
</blockquote>

Sampan Nettayanun from [[Naresuan University]] traces the concept, if not the terminology, as far back as [[Andrew Carnegie]], in his decision to concentrate on [[iron]] and [[steel]], writing "My advice to young men would be not only to concentrate their whole time and attention on the one business in life in which they engage, but to put every dollar of their capital into it."<ref name="n">{{cite journal|last1=Nettayanun|first1=Sampan|date=October 2016|title=Value investing: Circle of competence in the Thai insurance industry|journal=Puey Ungphakorn Institute for Economic Research|volume=46}}</ref>{{rp|3}}

Operating within one's circle of competence may be compared with those who act over-confidently. For example, [[institutional investors]] who have been successful in the past are more likely to attribute their success to their own abilities, rather than external forces, and are therefore more likely to make investments in areas outside their circle of competence.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nguyen|first1=Tristan|last2=Schüßler|first2=Alexander|title=Investment decisions and socio-demographic characteristics – Empirical evidence from Germany|journal=International Journal of Economics and Finance|date=2012|volume=4|issue=9|page=2|doi=10.5539/ijef.v4n9p1|doi-access=free}}</ref> The strategy of operating within their individual circles has been cited as the reason both Buffett and Munger avoided investing in the technology sector.<ref>{{cite web|title=Charlie Munger: The power of not making stupid decisions|url=http://www.hitc.com/en-gb/2017/08/04/charlie-munger-the-power-of-not-making-stupid-decisions/|website=HITC|publisher=[[CNBC]]|accessdate=13 January 2018}}</ref>

The breadth of any individual's circle of competence may be determined by a range of factors, including their [[profession]], spending habits, and the types of products they normally use. Remaining within one's circle confers a number of benefits, such as an unfair information advantage, the narrowing of available options, and the reduction of poor decision making.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Ang|first1=Rusmin|title=3 reasons why you should stay within your circle of competence|url=https://fifthperson.com/3-reasons-why-you-should-stay-within-your-circle-of-competence/|website=The Fifth Person|accessdate=13 January 2018|date=September 2, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ang|first1=Rusmin|last2=Chng|first2=Victor|title=Value Investing in Growth Companies: How to Spot High Growth Businesses and Generate 40% to 400% Investment Returns|date=Apr 23, 2013|publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]]|isbn=9781118567791|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lHZHHSKUSbUC|accessdate=13 January 2018}}</ref>
